Chardin, who was so long in the East, and observed their customs with so much care, supposed, in a manuscript note on <reference osisRef="Gen.43.11">Gen 43:11</reference>, that the balm and the honey sent by Jacob into Egypt for a present were carried in a goat or kid's skin, in which all sorts of things, both dry and liquid, are wont to be carried in the East. "Understood after this manner, the passage promises Israel success in their commerce, as the next verse (the 6th) promises them personal safety in their going out and in their return. In this view the passage appears with due distinctness, and a noble extent." - Observations, vol. 2:, p. 181.
entries.7f62c153c463f7691eefe94de12455b52784da00: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen7017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7018" type="x-p"/> When thou comest in - From thy employment, thou shalt find that no evil has happened to the family or dwelling in thy absence. <div eID="gen7018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7019" type="x-p"/> When thou goest out - Thy way shall be made prosperous before thee, and thou shalt have the Divine blessing in all thy labors.
entries.b8eec061d2fd78d04646661e642d21d9a8ba696f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen7019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7020" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall cause thine enemies, etc. - This is a promise of security from foreign invasion, or total discomfiture of the invaders, should they enter the land. They shall come against thee one way - in the firmest and most united manner. And flee seven ways - shall be utterly broken, confounded, and finally routed.
entries.5d54ead793b4c4419ad44e161a1b05848cbf5ec6: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen7020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7021" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall command the blessing upon thee - Every thing that thou hast shall come by Divine appointment; thou shalt have nothing casually, but every thing, both spiritual and temporal, shall come by the immediate command of God.
entries.055280ed12d90c25e5f408e34c8cba875a9bc11c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen7021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7022" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall establish thee a holy people unto himself - This is the sum of all blessings, to be made holy, and be preserved in holiness. <div eID="gen7022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7023" type="x-p"/> If thou shalt keep, etc. - Here is the solemn condition; if they did not keep God's testimonies, taking them for the regulators of their lives, and according to their direction walking in his ways, under the influence and aids of his grace, then the curses, and not the blessings, must be their portion. See <reference osisRef="Deu.28.15">Deu 28:15</reference>, etc.
entries.722c51473ab369a3ec0c685116065cdfaf5fe098: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen7023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7024" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall open unto thee his good treasure - The clouds, so that a sufficiency of fructifying showers should descend at all requisite times, and the vegetative principle in the earth should unfold and exert itself, so that their crops should be abundant.
entries.c3056056a6974ba56ee1816f806931ab9fc4103c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen7024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7025" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not go aside - to the right hand or to the left - The way of obedience is a straight way; it goes right forward; he who declines either to right or left from this path goes astray and misses heaven.
entries.a59efc5f1cdb0f5840d0ed93e30c2b0d9aa6c800: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen7025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7026" type="x-p"/> Cursing - This shall be thy state; vexation - grief, trouble, and anguish of heart; rebuke - continual judgments, and marks of God's displeasure.
entries.0a03a763e06c6af7b61f52e2ca5bf5bc54c75205: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen7026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7027" type="x-p"/> The pestilence cleave unto thee - ידבק יהוה בך אה הדבר yadbek Yehovah becha eth haddaber, the Lord shall cement the pestilence or plague to thee. Sept., Προσκολλησει Κυριος εις σε τον θανατον, The Lord will glue - inseparably attach, the death unto thee. How dreadful a plague it must be that ravages without intermission, any person may conceive who has ever heard the name.
entries.490634bc92951359894bab9f7691878c848e68af: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen7027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7028" type="x-p"/> Consumption - שחפת shachepheth, atrophy through lack of food; from שחף shacaph, to be in want. <div eID="gen7028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7029" type="x-p"/> Fever - קדחת kaddachath, from קדח kadach, to be kindled, burn, sparkle; a burning inflammatory fever. <div eID="gen7029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7030" type="x-p"/> Inflammation - דלקת dalleketh, from דלק dalak, to pursue eagerly, to burn after; probably a rapidly consuming cancer. <div eID="gen7030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7031" type="x-p"/> Extreme burning - חרחר charchur, burning upon burning, scald upon scald; from חר char, to be heated, enraged, etc. This probably refers, not only to excruciating inflammations on the body, but also to the irritation and agony of a mind utterly abandoned by God, and lost to hope. What an accumulation of misery! how formidable! and especially in a land where great heat was prevalent and dreadful. <div eID="gen7031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7032" type="x-p"/> Sword - War in general, enemies without, and civil broils within. This was remarkably the case in the last siege of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen7032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7033" type="x-p"/> Blasting - שדפון shiddaphon, probably either the blighting east wind that ruined vegetation, or those awful pestilential winds which suffocate both man and beast wherever they come. These often prevail in different parts of the East, and several examples have already been given. See <reference osisRef="Gen.41.6">Gen 41:6</reference> (note). <div eID="gen7033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7034" type="x-p"/> Mildew - ירקון yerakon, an exudation of the vegetative juice from different parts of the stalk, by which the maturity and perfection of the plant are utterly prevented. It comes from ירק yarak, to throw out moisture. <div eID="gen7034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7035" type="x-p"/> Of these seven plagues, the five former were to fall on their bodies, the two latter upon their substance. What a fearful thing it is to fall into the hands of the living God!
entries.1c314ebd309b34c82c57e73ccef5054e988e13ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen7035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7036" type="x-p"/> Thy heaven - shall be brass, and the earth - iron - The atmosphere should not be replenished with aqueous vapours, in consequence of which they should have neither the early nor the latter rain; hence the earth - the ground, must be wholly intractable, and, through its hardness, incapable of cultivation. God shows them by this that he is Lord of nature; and that drought and sterility are not casualties, but proceed from the immediate appointment of the Lord.
entries.b0e50eb588def38966e9ea22dbe4bbc851e91b33: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen7036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7037" type="x-p"/> The rain of thy land powder and dust - As their heavens - atmosphere, clouds, etc., were to be as brass - yielding no rain; so the surface of the earth must be reduced to powder; and this, being frequently taken up by the strong winds, would fall down in showers instead of rain. Whole caravans have been buried under showers of sand; and Thevenot, a French traveler, who had observed these showers of dust, etc., says, "They grievously annoy all they fall on, filling their eyes, ears, nostrils, etc." - Travels in the East, part 1, book ii., chap. 80. The ophthalmia in Egypt appears to be chiefly owing to a very fine sand, the particles of which are like broken glass, which are carried about by the wind, and, entering into the ciliary glands, produce grievous and continual inflammations.
entries.5836f79f151a83bb364909d8ffd34bc8edfaac87: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen7037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7038" type="x-p"/> The Lord will smite thee with the botch - שחין shechin, a violent inflammatory swelling. In Job ii., one of the Hexapla versions renders it ελεφας, the elephantiasis, a disease the most horrid that can possibly afflict human nature. In this disorder, the whole body is covered with a most loathsome scurf; the joints are all preternaturally enlarged, and the skin swells up and grows into folds like that of an elephant, whence the disease has its name. The skin, through its rigidity, breaks across at all the joints, and a most abominable ichor flows from all the chinks, etc. See an account of it in Aretaeus, whose language is sufficient to chill the blood of a maniac, could he attend to the description given by this great master, of this most loathsome and abominable of all the natural productions of death and sin. This was called the botch of Egypt, as being peculiar to that country, and particularly in the vicinity of the Nile. Hence those words of Lucretius: - <div eID="gen7038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7039" type="x-p"/> Est Elephas morbus, qui circum flumina Nili <div eID="gen7039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7040" type="x-p"/> Nascitur, Aegypto in media; nec praeterea usquam. <div eID="gen7040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7041" type="x-p"/> Lib. vi., ver. 1112. <div eID="gen7041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7042" type="x-p"/> Emerods - עפלים ophalim, from עפל aphal, to be elevated, raised up; swellings, protuberances; probably the bleeding piles. <div eID="gen7042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7043" type="x-p"/> Scab - brg garab does not occur as a verb in the Hebrew Bible, but gharb, in Arabic, signifies a distemper in the corner of the eye, (Castel)., and may amount to the Egyptian ophthalmia, which is so epidemic and distressing in that country: some suppose the scurvy to be intended. <div eID="gen7043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7044" type="x-p"/> Itch - חרס cheres, a burning itch, probably something of the erysipelatous kind, or what is commonly called St. Anthony's fire. <div eID="gen7044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7045" type="x-p"/> Whereof thou canst not be healed - For as they were inflicted by God's justice, they could not of course be cured by human art.
entries.f7f38e7db9fb23ed64fe65b523bf22d983a817eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen7045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7046" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall smite thee with madness - שגעון shiggaon, distraction, so that thou shalt not know what to do. <div eID="gen7046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7047" type="x-p"/> And blindness - עורון ivvaron, blindness, both physical and mental; the גרב garab, (<reference osisRef="Deu.28.27">Deu 28:27</reference>), destroying their eyes, and the judgments of God confounding their understandings. <div eID="gen7047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7048" type="x-p"/> Astonishment - תמהון timmahon, stupidity and amazement. By the just judgments of God they were so completely confounded, as not to discern the means by which they might prevent or remove their calamities, and to adopt those which led directly to their ruin. How true is the ancient saying, Quos Deus vult perdere, prius dementat! "Those whom God is determined to destroy, he first infatuates." But this applies not exclusively to the poor Jews: how miserably infatuated have the powers of the continent of Europe been, in all their councils and measures, for several years past! And what is the result? They have fallen - most deplorably fallen!
entries.8ba216d37421517e73adb3ac9f7ace45fd7514eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen7048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7049" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt be only oppressed, etc. - Perhaps no people under the sun have been more oppressed and spoiled than the rebellious Jews. Indeed, this has been their portion, with but little intermission, for nearly 1,800 years. And still they grope at noon day, as the blind gropeth in darkness - they do not yet discover, notwithstanding the effulgence of the light by which they are encompassed, that the rejection of their own Messiah is the cause of all their calamities.
entries.e0b3587484b0408cfc774d18b5ecf4073b4dcbc0: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen7049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7050" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt betroth a wife, etc. - Can any heart imagine any thing more grievous than the evils threatened in this and the following verses? To be on the brink of all social and domestic happiness, and then to be suddenly deprived of all, and see an enemy possess and enjoy every thing that was dear to them, must excite them to the utmost pitch of distraction and madness. They have, it is true, grievously sinned; but, O ye Christians, have they not grievously suffered for it? Is not the stroke of God heavy enough upon them? Do not then, by unkind treatment or cruel Oppression, increase their miseries. They are, above all others, the men who have seen affliction by the stroke of his rod; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.1">Lam 3:1</reference>.
entries.4e29f225a6621bc55f4e5472bf6a381613e88461: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen7050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7051" type="x-p"/> Thy sons and thy daughters shall be given unto another people - In several countries, particularly in Spain and Portugal, the children of the Jews have been taken from them by order of government, and educated in the Popish faith. There have been some instances of Jewish children being taken from their parents even in Protestant countries.
entries.cf0ebad40cdee9f0631574615879978b0102a662: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen7051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7052" type="x-p"/> With a sore botch - שחין shechin, an inflammatory swelling, a burning boil. See <reference osisRef="Deu.28.27">Deu 28:27</reference>.
entries.f4fdef71d701e3e751cc6a98f4872e05394f52bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen7052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7053" type="x-p"/> Can any thing be conceived more dreadful than the calamities threatened in these verses?
entries.dc7df04b841b011b8e8eaef6c5285281b941c2ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen7053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7054" type="x-p"/> Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies - Because they would not serve God, therefore they became slaves to men.
entries.068d90f92654ba6c1d00168015abdf799e5ada61: <hi type="bold">Verse 49</hi> <div eID="gen7054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7055" type="x-p"/> A nation - from far - Probably the Romans. <div eID="gen7055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7056" type="x-p"/> As the eagle flieth - The very animal on all the Roman standards. The Roman eagle is proverbial. <div eID="gen7056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7057" type="x-p"/> Whose tongue thou shalt not understand - The Latin language, than which none was more foreign to the structure and idiom of the Hebrew.
entries.3ba8f45da1034a7dc85a9926d06addb25f6621d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 52</hi> <div eID="gen7057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7058" type="x-p"/> He - Nebuchadnezzar first, (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1">2Kgs 25:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.2">2Kgs 25:2</reference>, etc)., and Titus next; shall besiege thee - beset thee round on every side, and cast a trench around thee: viz., lines of circumvallation, as our Lord predicted; (see <reference osisRef="Mat.24.1">Mat 24:1</reference>, etc., and <reference osisRef="Luk.21.5">Luk 21:5</reference>, etc.); in all thy gates throughout all thy land - all thy fenced cities, which points out that their subjugation should be complete, as both Jerusalem and all their fortified places should be taken. This was done literally by Nebuchadnezzar and the Romans.
entries.92bb41ca501bba581f1cd283ef5e5b059b101723: <hi type="bold">Verse 56</hi> <div eID="gen7058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7059" type="x-p"/> The tender and delicate woman - This was literally fulfilled when Jerusalem was besieged by the Romans; a woman named Mary, of a noble family, driven to distraction by famine, boiled and ate her own child! See a similar case <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.29">2Kgs 6:29</reference> (note); and <reference osisRef="Lev.26.29">Lev 26:29</reference> (note).
entries.316c518e02bd19dd2026fbd7a42934a67bd8f3ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 57</hi> <div eID="gen7059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7060" type="x-p"/> Toward her young one - and toward her children which she shall bear - There seems to be a species of tautology in the two clauses of this verse, which may be prevented by translating the last word, שליתה shilyathah, literally, her secondines, which is the meaning of the Arabic sala, not badly understood by the Septuagint, χοριον αυτης, the chorion or exterior membrane, which invests the fetus in the womb; and still better translated by Luther, the after-birth; which saying of Moses strongly marks the deepest distress, when the mother is represented as feeling the most poignant regret that her child was brought forth into such a state of suffering and death; and 2dly, that it was likely, from the favorable circumstances after the birth, that she herself should survive her inlaying. No words can more forcibly depict the miseries of those dreadful times. On this ground I see no absolute need for Kennicott's criticism, who, instead of ובשליתה ubeshilyathah, against her secondines, reads ובשלה ubashelah, and she shall boll, and translates the 56th and 57th verses as follows: "The tender and delicate woman among you, who would not adventure to set the sole of her foot upon the ground for delicateness and tenderness, her eye shall be evil toward the husband of her bosom, and toward her son, and toward her daughter. 57. And she shall boil that which cometh out from between her feet, even her children, which she shall bear, for she shall eat them, for want of all things, secretly." These words, says he, being prophetical, are fulfilled in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.29">2Kgs 6:29</reference>, for we read there that two women of Samaria having agreed to eat their own children, one was actually boiled, where the very same word, בשל bashal is used. See Kennicott's Dissertations on 1 Chronicles 11, etc., p. 421.
entries.7ae28e674f58a63dc041937caf414f8ac2163746: <hi type="bold">Verse 64</hi> <div eID="gen7060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7061" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall scatter thee among all people - How literally has this been fulfilled! The people of the Jews are scattered over every nation under heaven.
entries.b685d71db69c5f256db8ec256d2073b5df1f84c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 65</hi> <div eID="gen7061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7062" type="x-p"/> No ease - a trembling heart, and failing of eyes - The trembling of heart may refer to their state of continual insecurity, being, under every kind of government, proscribed, and, even under the most mild, uncertain of toleration and protection; and the failing of eyes, to their vain and ever-disappointed expectation of the Messiah.
entries.951b6fe38c61abad8a6b7b557678896c11427876: <hi type="bold">Verse 68</hi> <div eID="gen7062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7063" type="x-p"/> And the Lord shall bring thee into Egypt again - That is, into another state of slavery and bondage similar to that of Egypt, out of which they had been lately brought. And there ye shall be sold, that is, be exposed to sale, or expose yourself to sale as the word התמכרתם hithmaccartem may be rendered; they were vagrants, and wished to become slaves that they might be provided with the necessaries of life. And no man shall buy you; even the Romans thought it a reproach to have a Jew for a slave, they had become so despicable to all mankind. When Jerusalem was taken by Titus, many of the captives, which were above seventeen years of age, were sent into the works in Egypt. See Josephus, Antiq., b. xii, 100:1, 2, War b. vi., c. 9, s. 2; and above all, see Bp. Newton's Dissertations on the Prophecies. <div eID="gen7063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7064" type="x-p"/> The first verse of the next chapter, in some of the most correct Hebrew Bibles, makes the 69th of this; and very properly, as the second verse of the following chapter begins a new subject. <div eID="gen7064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7065" type="x-p"/> This is an astonishing chapter: in it are prophecies delivered more than 3,000 years ago, and now fulfilling. <div eID="gen7065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7066" type="x-p"/> O God, how immense is thy wisdom, and how profound thy counsels! To thee alone are known all thy works from the beginning to the end. What an irrefragable proof does this chapter, compared with the past and present state of the Jewish people, afford of the truth and Divine origin of the Pentateuch!  <chapter eID="Deut.28"/> <div eID="gen7066" type="x-p"/>

entries.cf81121c1957b24123169da77647a8a16b99eb94: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.1-Deut.28.6">Deu 28:1-6</reference> <div eID="gen2476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2477" type="x-p"/> The Blessing. - Deu 28:1. If Israel would hearken to the voice of the Lord its God, the Lord would make it the highest of all the nations of the earth. This thought, with which the discourse on the law in <reference osisRef="Deut.26.19">Deu 26:19</reference> terminated, forms the theme, and in a certain sense the heading, of the following description of the blessing, through which the Lord, according to the more distinct declaration in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.2">Deu 28:2</reference>, would glorify His people above all the nations of the earth. The indispensable condition for obtaining this blessing, was obedience to the word of the Lord, or keeping His commandments. To impress this <hi type="italic">condition sine qua non</hi> thoroughly upon the people, Moses not only repeats it at the commencement (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.2">Deu 28:2</reference>), and in the middle (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.9">Deu 28:9</reference>), but also at the close (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.13">Deu 28:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.14">Deu 28:14</reference>), in both a positive and a negative form. In <reference osisRef="Deut.28.2">Deu 28:2</reference>, “the way in which Israel was to be exalted is pointed out” (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>); and thus the theme is more precisely indicated, and the elaboration of it is introduced. “All these blessings (those mentioned singly in what follows) will come upon thee and reach thee.” The blessings are represented as actual powers, which follow the footsteps of the nation, and overtake it. In <reference osisRef="Deut.28.3-Deut.28.6">Deu 28:3-6</reference>, the fulness of the blessing of God in all the relations of life is depicted in a sixfold repetition of the word “blessed.” Israel will be blessed in the town and in the field, the two spheres in which its life moves (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.3">Deu 28:3</reference>); blessed will be the fruit of the body, of the earth, and of the cattle, i.e., in all its productions (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.4">Deu 28:4</reference>; for each one, see <reference osisRef="Deut.7.13-Deut.7.14">Deu 7:13-14</reference>); blessed will be the basket (<reference osisRef="Deut.26.2">Deu 26:2</reference>) in which the fruits are kept, and the kneading - trough (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.34">Exo 12:34</reference>) in which the daily bread is prepared (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.5">Deu 28:5</reference>); blessed will the nation be in all its undertakings (“coming in and going out;” vid., Num 27:17).
entries.4b024134aba57d84a136d0f1832953322e64f142: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.7-Deut.28.14">Deu 28:7-14</reference> <div eID="gen2477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2478" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Deut.28.7-Deut.28.14">Deu 28:7-14</reference> describe the influence and effect of the blessing upon all the circumstances and situations in which the nation might be placed: in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.7-Deut.28.10">Deu 28:7-10</reference>, with reference (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) to the attitude of Israel towards its enemies (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.7">Deu 28:7</reference>); (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) to its trade and handicraft (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.8">Deu 28:8</reference>); (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) to its attitude towards all the nations of the earth (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.9">Deu 28:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.10">Deu 28:10</reference>). The optative forms, יתּן and יצו (in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.7">Deu 28:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.28.8">Deu 28:8</reference>), are worthy of notice. They show that Moses not only proclaimed the blessing to the people, but desired it for them, because he knew that Israel would not always or perfectly fulfil the condition upon which it was to be bestowed. “<hi type="italic">May the Lord be pleased to give thine enemies...smitten before thee</hi>,” i.e., give them up to thee as smitten (לפני נתן, to give up before a person, to deliver up to him: cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.1.8">Deu 1:8</reference>), so that they shall come out against thee by one way, and flee from thee by seven ways, i.e., in wild dispersion (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.7-Lev.26.8">Lev 26:7-8</reference>).
entries.7dc87d33cb3aecff64227e14e0f46476031667ef: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.8">Deu 28:8</reference> <div eID="gen2478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2479" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">May the Lord command the blessing with thee</hi> (put it at thy disposal) <hi type="italic">in thy barns</hi> (granaries, store-rooms) <hi type="italic">and in all thy business</hi>” (“to set the hand;” see <reference osisRef="Deut.12.7">Deu 12:7</reference>).
entries.1c9129fb52c86fa5cd3fc5c10ef0e26b8c728b2c: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.9-Deut.28.12">Deu 28:9-12</reference> <div eID="gen2479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2480" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">The Lord will exalt thee for a holy nation to Himself,...so that all the nations of the earth shall see that the name of Jehovah is named upon thee, and shall fear before thee</hi>.” The Lord had called Israel as a holy nation, when He concluded the covenant with it (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5-Exod.19.6">Exo 19:5-6</reference>). This promise, to which the words “as He hath sworn unto thee” point back, and which is called an oath, because it was founded upon the promises given to the patriarchs on oath (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.16">Gen 22:16</reference>), and was given implicite in them, the Lord would fulfil to His people, and cause the holiness and glory of Israel to be so clearly manifested, that all nations should perceive or see “<hi type="italic">that the name of the Lord is named upon Israel</hi>.” The name of the Lord is the revelation of His glorious nature. It is named upon Israel, when Israel is transformed into the glory of the divine nature (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.63.19">Isa 63:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.9">Jer 14:9</reference>). It was only in feeble commencements that this blessing was fulfilled upon Israel under the Old Testament; and it is not till the restoration of Israel, which is to take place in the future according to Rom 11:25., that its complete fulfilment will be attained. In <reference osisRef="Deut.28.11">Deu 28:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.28.12">Deu 28:12</reference>, Moses returns to the earthly blessing, for the purpose of unfolding this still further. “<hi type="italic">Superabundance will the Lord give thee for good</hi> (i.e., for happiness and prosperity; vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.30.9">Deu 30:9</reference>), <hi type="italic">in fruit of thy body</hi>,” etc. (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.28.4">Deu 28:4</reference>). He would open His good treasure-house, the heaven, to give rain to the land in its season (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.11.14">Deu 11:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.4-Lev.26.5">Lev 26:4-5</reference>), and bless the work of the hands, i.e., the cultivation of the soil, so that Israel would be able to lend to many, according to the prospect already set before it in Deu 15:6.
entries.7126aa79582916d3250f8e646ff327166f964690: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.13-Deut.28.14">Deu 28:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen2480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2481" type="x-p"/> By such blessings He would “<hi type="italic">make Israel the head, and not the tail</hi>,” - a figure taken from life (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Isa 9:13</reference>), the meaning of which is obvious, and is given literally in the next sentence, “<hi type="italic">thou wilt be above only, and not beneath</hi>,” i.e., thou wilt rise more and more, and increase in wealth, power, and dignity. With this the discourse returns to its commencement; and the promise of blessing closes with another emphatic repetition of the condition on which the fulfilment depended (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Deut.28.13">Deu 28:13</reference></hi> and Deu 28:14. On <reference osisRef="Deut.28.14">Deu 28:14</reference>, see <reference osisRef="Deut.5.29">Deu 5:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.28">Deu 11:28</reference>). <div eID="gen2481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2482" type="x-p"/> The Curse, in case Israel should not hearken to the voice of its God, to keep His commandments. After the announcement that all these (the following) curses would come upon the disobedient nation (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.15">Deu 28:15</reference>), the curse is proclaimed in all its extent, as covering all the relations of life, in a sixfold repetition of the word “cursed” (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.16-Deut.28.19">Deu 28:16-19</reference>, as above in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.3-Deut.28.6">Deu 28:3-6</reference>); and the fulfilment of this threat in plagues and diseases, drought and famine, war, devastation of the land, and captivity of the people, is so depicted, that the infliction of these punishments stands out to view in ever increasing extent and fearfulness. We are not to record this, however, as a gradual heightening of the judgments of God, in proportion to the increasing rebellion of Israel, as in Lev 26:14., although it is obvious that the punishments threatened did not fall upon the nation all at once.
entries.8ba7154173aef1167d30b85582b4ba4e10671745: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.16-Deut.28.19">Deu 28:16-19</reference> <div eID="gen2482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2483" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Deut.28.16-Deut.28.19">Deu 28:16-19</reference> correspond precisely to <reference osisRef="Deut.28.3-Deut.28.6">Deu 28:3-6</reference>, so as to set forth the curse as the counterpart of the blessing, except that the basket and kneading-trough are mentioned before the fruit of the body.
entries.144b5e4ab68fe23bb8c158688209265255af9e96: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.20-Deut.28.22">Deu 28:20-22</reference> <div eID="gen2483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2484" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">first</hi> view, in which the bursting of the threatened curse upon the disobedient people is proclaimed in all its forms. First of all, quite generally in Deu 28:20. “<hi type="italic">The Lord will send the curse against thee, consternation and threatening in every undertaking of thy hand which thou carriest out</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Deut.12.7">Deu 12:7</reference>), <hi type="italic">till thou be destroyed, till thou perish quickly, because of the wickedness of thy doings, because thou hast forsaken Me</hi>.” The three words, מארה, מהוּמה, and מגערת, are synonymous, and are connected together to strengthen the thought. מארה, curse or malediction; המּהוּמה, the consternation produced by the curse of God, namely, the confusion with which God smites His foes (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.7.23">Deu 7:23</reference>); המּגערה is the threatening word of the divine wrath. - Then Deu 28:21. in detail. “<hi type="italic">The Lord will make the pestilence fasten upon</hi> (cleave to) <hi type="italic">thee, till He hath destroyed thee out of the land...to smite thee with giddiness and fever</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">Lev 26:16</reference>), <hi type="italic">inflammation, burning, and sword, blasting of corn, and mildew </hi>(of the seed);” seven diseases therefore (seven as the stamp of the words of God), whilst pestilence in particular is mentioned first, as the most terrible enemy of life. דּלּקת, from דּלק to burn, and חרחר, from חרר to glow, signify inflammatory diseases, burning fevers; the distinction between these and קדּחת cannot be determined. Instead of חרב, the sword as the instrument of death, used to designate slaughter and death, the <hi type="italic">Vulgate</hi>, <hi type="italic">Arabic</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Samaritan</hi> have adopted the reading חרב, <hi type="italic">aestus</hi>, heat (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.40">Gen 31:40</reference>), or drought, according to which there would be four evils mentioned by which human life is attacked, and three which are injurious to the corn. But as the lxx, <hi type="italic">Jon</hi>., <hi type="italic">Syr</hi>., and others read חרב, this alteration is very questionable, especially as the reading can be fully defended in this connection; and one objection to the alteration is, that drought is threatened for the first time in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.23">Deu 28:23</reference>, Deu 28:24. שׁדּפון, from שׁדף to singe or blacken, and ירקון, from ירק to be yellowish, refer to two diseases which attack the corn: the former to the withering or burning of the ears, caused by the east wind (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.23">Gen 41:23</reference>); the other to the effect produced by a warm wind in Arabia, by which the green ears are turned yellow, so that they bear no grains of corn.
entries.5abf0ec50279f42cfa8e16735ddbe7cd85b42bfc: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.23-Deut.28.24">Deu 28:23-24</reference> <div eID="gen2484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2485" type="x-p"/> To this should be added terrible drought, without a drop of rain from heaven (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.19">Lev 26:19</reference>). Instead of rain, dust and ashes should fall from heaven. נתן construed with a double accusative: to make the rain of the land into dust and ashes, to give it in the form of dust and ashes. When the heat is very great, the air in Palestine is often full of dust and sand, the wind assuming the form of a burning sirocco, so that the air resembles the glowing heat at the mouth of a furnace (Robinson, ii. 504).
entries.d261eccb42f575e9455ca6e7dbeb07082d4bb05c: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.25-Deut.28.26">Deu 28:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen2485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2486" type="x-p"/> Defeat in battle, the very opposite of the blessing promised in Deu 28:7. Israel should become לזעוה, “<hi type="italic">a moving to and fro</hi>,” i.e., so to speak, “a ball for all the kingdoms of the earth to play with” (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>). זעוה, here and at <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.46">Eze 23:46</reference>, is not a transposed and later form of זועה, which has a different meaning in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.19">Isa 28:19</reference>, but the original uncontracted form, which was afterwards condensed into זועה; for this, and not זועה, is the way in which the <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> should be read in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.4">Jer 15:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.24.9">Jer 24:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.18">Jer 29:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.17">Jer 34:17</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.8">2Ch 29:8</reference>, where this threat is repeated (vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §53, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.). The corpses of those who were slain by the foe should serve as food for the birds of prey and wild beasts - the greatest ignominy that could fall upon the dead, and therefore frequently held out as a threat against the ungodly (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.33">Jer 7:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.4">Jer 16:4</reference>; 1Ki 14:11, etc.).
entries.369fd4da6b062beb9f9c26900cf6fcfc7402e12c: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.27-Deut.28.34">Deu 28:27-34</reference> <div eID="gen2486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2487" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">second</hi> view depicts still further the visitation of God both by diseases of body and soul, and also by plunder and oppression on the part of their enemies. - In <reference osisRef="Deut.28.27">Deu 28:27</reference> four incurable diseases of the body are threatened: the ulcer of Egypt (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.9.9">Exo 9:9</reference>), i.e., the form of leprosy peculiar to Egypt, <hi type="italic">elephantiasis</hi> (<hi type="italic">Aegypti peculiare malum:</hi> <hi type="italic">Plin</hi>. xxvi. c. 1, s. 5), which differed from <hi type="italic">lepra tuberosa</hi>, however, or tubercular leprosy (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.35">Deu 28:35</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Job.2.7">Job 2:7</reference>), in degree only, and not in its essential characteristics (see <hi type="italic">Tobler, mediz. Topogr. v. Jerus. </hi>p. 51). עפלים, from עפל, a swelling, rising, signifies a tumour, and according to the Rabbins a disease of the anus: in men, <hi type="italic">tumor in posticis partibus;</hi> in women, <hi type="italic">durius quoddam</hi> οἴδημα <hi type="italic">in utero</hi>. It was with this disease that the Philistines were smitten (<reference osisRef="1Sam.5.1-1Sam.5.12">1Sa 5:1-12</reference>). גּרב (see <reference osisRef="Lev.21.20">Lev 21:20</reference>) and חרס, from חרס, to scrape or scratch, also a kind of itch, of which there are several forms in Syria and Egypt.
entries.d5f0152e6d3dde7c1cedfe21ba2ed02fa910a3f9: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.28-Deut.28.29">Deu 28:28-29</reference> <div eID="gen2487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2488" type="x-p"/> In addition to this, there would come idiocy, blindness, and confusion of mind, - three psychical maladies; for although עוּרון signifies primarily bodily blindness, the position of the word between idiocy and confusion of heart, i.e., of the understanding, points to mental blindness here.
entries.be30f1c29f786e0f9a67a3e1687df5a282f88bb6: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.29-Deut.28.34">Deu 28:29-34</reference> <div eID="gen2488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2489" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Deut.28.29">Deu 28:29</reference> leads to the same conclusion, where it is stated that Israel would grope in the bright noon-day, like a blind man in the dark, and not make his ways prosper, i.e., not hit upon the right road which led to the goal and to salvation, would have no good fortune or success in its undertakings (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference>). Being thus smitten in body and soul, it would be <hi type="italic">only</hi> (אך as in <reference osisRef="Deut.16.15">Deu 16:15</reference>), i.e., utterly, oppressed and spoiled evermore. These words introduce the picture of the other calamity, viz., the plundering of the nation and the land by enemies (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.30-Deut.28.33">Deu 28:30-33</reference>). Wife, house, vineyard, ox, ass, and sheep would be taken away by the foe; sons and daughters would be carried away into captivity before the eyes of the people, who would see it and pine after the children, i.e., with sorrow and longing after them; “<hi type="italic">and thy hand shall not be to thee towards God</hi>,” i.e., all power and help will fail thee. (On this proverbial expression, see <reference osisRef="Gen.31.29">Gen 31:29</reference>; and on חלּל, in <reference osisRef="Gen.31.30">Gen 31:30</reference>, see at Deu 20:6.) - In <reference osisRef="Deut.28.33">Deu 28:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.34">Deu 28:34</reference>, this threat is summed up in the following manner: the fruit of the field and all their productions would be devoured by a strange nation, and Israel would be only oppressed and crushed to pieces all its days, and become mad on account of what its eyes would be compelled to see.
entries.62e972d8e50d79430d56f885c550fd2e1be8e1f8: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.35-Deut.28.46">Deu 28:35-46</reference> <div eID="gen2489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2490" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">third</hi> view. - With the words, “<hi type="italic">the Lord will smite thee</hi>,” Moses resumes in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.35">Deu 28:35</reference> the threat of <reference osisRef="Deut.28.27">Deu 28:27</reference>, to set forth the calamities already threatened under a new aspect, namely, as signs of the rejection of Israel from covenant fellowship with the Lord. <div eID="gen2490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2491" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Deut.28.35">Deu 28:35</reference> <div eID="gen2491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2492" type="x-p"/> The Lord would smite the people with grievous abscesses in the knees and thighs, that should be incurable, even from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head. רע שׁחין ר is the so-called joint-leprosy, a form of the <hi type="italic">lepra tuberosa</hi> (vid., <hi type="italic">Pruner</hi>, p. 167). From the clause, however, “<hi type="italic">from the sole of thy foot unto the top of thy head</hi>,” it is evident that the threat is not to be restricted to this species of leprosy, since “the upper parts of the body often remain in a perfectly normal state in cases of leprosy in the joints; and after the diseased parts have fallen off, the patients recover their previous health to a certain degree” (<hi type="italic">Pruner</hi>). Moses mentions this as being a disease of such a nature, that it would render it utterly impossible for those who were afflicted with it either to stand or walk, and then heightens the threat by adding the words, “from the sole of the foot to the top of the head.” Leprosy excluded from fellowship with the Lord, and deprived the nation of the character of a nation of God.
entries.7ad9d52bd69d05545bd99fd49640606bd54b3b89: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.36-Deut.28.37">Deu 28:36-37</reference> <div eID="gen2492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2493" type="x-p"/> The loss of their spiritual character would be followed by the dissolution of the covenant fellowship. This thought connects <reference osisRef="Deut.28.36">Deu 28:36</reference> with <reference osisRef="Deut.28.35">Deu 28:35</reference>, and not the thought that Israel being afflicted with leprosy would be obliged to go into captivity, and in this state would become an object of abhorrence to the heathen (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>). The Lord would bring the nation and its king to a foreign nation that it did not know, and thrust them into bondage, so that it would be obliged to serve other gods - wood and stone (vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.4.28">Deu 4:28</reference>), - and would become an object of disgust, a proverb, and a byword to all nations whither God should drive it (vid., 1Ki 9:7; <reference osisRef="Jer.24.9">Jer 24:9</reference>).
entries.79de19b79eefdeb087a8e9a9786f7fb25af266c2: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.38-Deut.28.39">Deu 28:38-39</reference> <div eID="gen2493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2494" type="x-p"/> Even in their own land the curse would fall upon every kind of labour and enterprise. Much seed would give little to reap, because the locust would devour the seed; the planting and dressing of the vineyard would furnish no wine to drink, because the worm would devour the vine. תּולעת is probably the ἴψ or ἴξ of the Greeks, the <hi type="italic">convolvulus</hi> of the Romans, our vine-weevil.
entries.dd7cdf1b8b7007e5b8010454090416ba2a88f595: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.40">Deu 28:40</reference> <div eID="gen2494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2495" type="x-p"/> They would have many olive-trees in the land, but not anoint themselves with oil, because the olive-tree would be rooted out or plundered (ישּׁל, Niphal of שׁלל, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.19.5">Deu 19:5</reference>, not the Kal of נשׁל, which cannot be shown to have the intransitive meaning <hi type="italic">elabi</hi>).
entries.caaddb0102eda6e41be3631cf1e8402335d9f84f: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.41">Deu 28:41</reference> <div eID="gen2495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2496" type="x-p"/> Sons and daughters would they beget, but not keep, because they would have to go into captivity.
entries.0c13b58a264fefa8e5b494eb020c1905c1c74463: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.42">Deu 28:42</reference> <div eID="gen2496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2497" type="x-p"/> All the trees and fruits of the land would the buzzer take possession of. צלצל, from צלל to <hi type="italic">buzz</hi>, a rhetorical epithet applied to <hi type="italic">locusts</hi>, not the grasshopper, which does not injure the fruits of the tree or ground sufficiently for the term ירשׁ, “to take possession of,” to be applicable to it.
entries.a5d7d52ea882dbb8bb082bbe5291b19a4eca1fc5: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.43">Deu 28:43</reference> <div eID="gen2497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2498" type="x-p"/> Israel would be utterly impoverished, and would sink lower and lower, whilst the stranger in the midst of it would, on the contrary, get above it very high; not indeed “because he had no possession, but was dependent upon resources of other kinds” (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>), but rather because he would be exempted with all his possessions from the curse of God, just as the Israelites had been exempted from the plagues which came upon the Egyptians (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.6-Exod.9.7">Exo 9:6-7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.26">Exo 9:26</reference>).
entries.a1fec0d89e3202490a3b2f5f581915407ee5826d: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.44-Deut.28.46">Deu 28:44-46</reference> <div eID="gen2498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2499" type="x-p"/> The opposite of <reference osisRef="Deut.28.12">Deu 28:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.28.13">Deu 28:13</reference> would come to pass. - In <reference osisRef="Deut.28.46">Deu 28:46</reference> the address returns to its commencement in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.15">Deu 28:15</reference>, with the terrible threat, “<hi type="italic">These curses shall be upon thee for a sign and for a wonder, and upon thy seed for ever</hi>,” for the purpose of making a pause, if not of bringing the whole to a close. The curses were for a sign and wonder (מופת, that which excites astonishment and terror), inasmuch as their magnitude and terrible character manifested most clearly the supernatural interposition of God (vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">Deu 29:23</reference>). “<hi type="italic">For ever</hi>” applies to the generation smitten by the curse, which would remain for ever rejected, though without involving the perpetual rejection of the whole nation, or the impossibility of the conversion and restoration of a remnant, or of a holy seed (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Isa 10:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">Isa 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.27">Rom 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Rom 11:5</reference>).
entries.b2bc7bec1d15907df7bb06fb1d11bf9e9d0a922b: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.47-Deut.28.57">Deu 28:47-57</reference> <div eID="gen2499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2500" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">fourth</hi> view. - Although in what precedes every side of the national life has been brought under the curse, yet love to his people, and the desire to preserve them from the curse, by holding up before them the dreadful severity of the wrath of God, impel the faithful servant of the Lord to go still further, and depict more minutely still the dreadful horrors consequent upon Israel being given up to the power of the heathen, and first of all in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.47-Deut.28.57">Deu 28:47-57</reference> the horrible calamities which would burst upon Israel on the conquest of the land and its fortresses by its foes.
entries.e6a44efd48fc6be59d80694c92629f4b1406b222: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.47-Deut.28.48">Deu 28:47-48</reference> <div eID="gen2500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2501" type="x-p"/> Because it had not served the Lord its God with joy and gladness of heart, “<hi type="italic">for the abundance of all</hi>,” i.e., for the abundance of all the blessings bestowed upon it by its God, it would serve its enemies in hunger, and thirst, and nakedness, and want of everything, and wear an iron yoke, i.e., be obliged to perform the hardest tributary service till it was destroyed (השׁמיד for השׁמיד, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.7.24">Deu 7:24</reference>).
entries.45050d8d9169edc41fb005190646385fb87b73ec: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.49-Deut.28.50">Deu 28:49-50</reference> <div eID="gen2501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2502" type="x-p"/> The Lord would bring against it from afar a barbarous, hardhearted nation, which knew not pity. “<hi type="italic">From afar</hi>” is still further strengthened by the addition of the words, “<hi type="italic">from the end of the earth</hi>.” The greater the distance off, the more terrible does the foe appear. He flies thence like an eagle, which plunges with violence upon its prey, and carries it off with its claws; and Israel does not understand its language, so as to be able to soften its barbarity, or come to any terms. A people “<hi type="italic">firm, hard of face,</hi>” i.e., upon whom nothing makes an impression (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">Isa 50:7</reference>), - a description of the audacity and shamelessness of its appearance (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.23">Dan 8:23</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.7.13">Pro 7:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.29">Pro 21:29</reference>), which spares neither old men nor boys. This description no doubt applies to the Chaldeans, who are described as flying eagles in Hab 1:6., <reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jer 48:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jer 49:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.7">Eze 17:7</reference>, as in the verses before us; but it applies to other enemies of Israel beside these, namely to the great imperial powers generally, the Assyrians, Chaldeans, and Romans, whom the Lord raised up as the executors of His curse upon His rebellious people. Isaiah therefore depicts the Assyrians in a similar manner, namely, as a people with an unintelligible language (<reference osisRef="Deut.5.26">Deu 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.11">Deu 28:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.19">Deu 33:19</reference>), and describes the cruelty of the Medes in <reference osisRef="Deut.13.17-Deut.13.18">Deu 13:17-18</reference>, with an unmistakeable allusion to <reference osisRef="Deut.28.50">Deu 28:50</reference> of the present threat.
entries.1657a0f43fc6549607e22d15ba089b25a6c83409: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.51-Deut.28.52">Deu 28:51-52</reference> <div eID="gen2502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2503" type="x-p"/> This foe would consume all the fruit of the cattle and the land, i.e., everything which the nation had acquired through agriculture and the breeding of stock, without leaving it anything, until it was utterly destroyed (see <reference osisRef="Deut.7.13">Deu 7:13</reference>), and would oppress, i.e., besiege it in all its gates (towns, vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.12.12">Deu 12:12</reference>), till the lofty and strong walls upon which they relied should fall (ירד as in <reference osisRef="Deut.20.20">Deu 20:20</reference>).
entries.98372c4dbf586f81d335e769cc1fd2c6d4b16e90: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.53">Deu 28:53</reference> <div eID="gen2503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2504" type="x-p"/> It would so distress Israel, that in their distress and siege they would be driven to eat the fruit of their body, and the flesh of their own children (with regard to the fulfilment of this, see the remarks on <reference osisRef="Lev.26.29">Lev 26:29</reference>). - This horrible distress is depicted still more fully in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.54-Deut.28.57">Deu 28:54-57</reference>, where the words, “<hi type="italic">in the siege and in the straitness</hi>,” etc. (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.53">Deu 28:53</reference>), are repeated as a <hi type="italic">refrain</hi>, with their appalling sound, in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.55">Deu 28:55</reference> and Deu 28:57.
entries.d33d7f123bf0c6dee5a302467878666c82e3ef04: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.54-Deut.28.55">Deu 28:54-55</reference> <div eID="gen2504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2505" type="x-p"/> The effeminate and luxurious man would look with ill-favour upon his brother, the wife of his bosom, and his remaining children, “to give” (so that he would not give) to one of them of the flesh of his children which he was consuming, because there was nothing left to him in the siege. “<hi type="italic">His eye shall be evil</hi>,” i.e., look with envy or ill-favour (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.15.9">Deu 15:9</reference>). השׁאיר מבּלי, on account of there not being anything left for himself. כּל with בּלי signifies literally “<hi type="italic">all not</hi>,” i.e., nothing at all. השׁאיר, an infinitive, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.3.3">Deu 3:3</reference> (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.28.48">Deu 28:48</reference>).
entries.89db14b2b9a031d76153c3a1c1a1e50d7a87ba1d: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.56-Deut.28.57">Deu 28:56-57</reference> <div eID="gen2505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2506" type="x-p"/> The delicate and luxurious woman, who had not attempted to put her feet to the ground (had always been carried therefore either upon a litter or an ass: cf. Jdg 5:10, and <hi type="italic">Arvieux, Sitten der Beduinen Ar.</hi> p. 143), from tenderness and delicacy - her eye would look with envy upon the husband of her bosom and her children, and that (<hi type="italic">vav expl</hi>.) because of (for) her after-birth, which cometh out from between her feet, and because of her children which she bears (sc., during the siege); “<hi type="italic">for she will eat them secretly in the want of everything</hi>,” that is to say, first of all attempt to appease her hunger with the after-birth, and then, when there was no more left, with her own children. To such an awful height would the famine rise!
entries.e87d28d093c87e18d43193f7a133705ae7c9fea9: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.58-Deut.28.68">Deu 28:58-68</reference> <div eID="gen2506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2507" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">fifth</hi> and last view. - And yet these horrible calamities would not be the end of the distress. The full measure of the divine curse would be poured out upon Israel, when its disobedience had become hardened into disregard of the glorious and fearful name of the Lord its God. To point this out, Moses describes the resistance of the people in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.58">Deu 28:58</reference>; not, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.15">Deu 28:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.28.45">Deu 28:45</reference>, as not hearkening to the voice of the Lord to keep all His commandments, which he (Moses) had commanded this day, or which Jehovah had commanded (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.45">Deu 28:45</reference>), but as “not observing to do all the words which are written in this book, to fear the glorified and fearful name,” (viz.) Jehovah its God. “<hi type="italic">This book</hi>” is not Deuteronomy, even if we should assume that Moses had not first of all delivered the discourses in this book to the people and then written them down, but had first of all written them down and then read them to the people (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.31.9">Deu 31:9</reference>), but the book of the law, i.e., the Pentateuch, so far as it was already written. This is evident from <reference osisRef="Deut.28.60">Deu 28:60</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.61">Deu 28:61</reference>, according to which the grievous diseases of Egypt were written in this book of the law, which points to the book of Exodus, where grievous diseases occur among the Egyptian plagues. In fact, Moses could not have thought of merely laying the people under the obligation to keep the laws of the book of Deuteronomy, since this book does not contain all the essential laws of the covenant, and was never intended to form an independent book of the law. The infinitive clause, “<hi type="italic">to fear</hi>,” etc., serves to explain the previous clause, “<hi type="italic">to do</hi>,” etc., whether we regard the two clauses as co-ordinate, or the second as subordinate to the first. Doing all the commandments of the law must show and prove itself in fearing the revealed name of the Lord. Where this fear is wanting, the outward observance of the commandments can only be a pharisaic work-righteousness, which is equivalent to a transgress of the law. But the object of this fear was not to be a God, according to human ideas of the nature and working of God; it was to be “<hi type="italic">this glorified and fearful name</hi>,” i.e., Jehovah the absolute God, as He glories Himself and shows Himself to be fearful in His doings upon earth. “<hi type="italic">The name</hi>,” as in Lev 24:11. נכבּד in a reflective sense, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.14.4">Exo 14:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.17-Exod.14.18">Exo 14:17-18</reference>; Lev 10:3.
entries.156db26b8a308a1aa1956a38297bda9a1f628bba: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.59-Deut.28.60">Deu 28:59-60</reference> <div eID="gen2507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2508" type="x-p"/> If Israel should not do this, the Lord would make its strokes and the strokes of its seed wonderful, i.e., would visit the people and their descendants with extraordinary strokes, with great and lasting strokes, and with evil and lasting diseases (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.60">Deu 28:60</reference>), and would bring all the pestilences of Egypt upon it. השׁיב, to turn back, inasmuch as Israel was set free from them by the deliverance out of Egypt. מדוה is construed with the plural as a collective noun.
entries.0bff7b80c51cf0961791e22bc49da8cc9278d035: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.61">Deu 28:61</reference> <div eID="gen2508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2509" type="x-p"/> Also every disease and every stroke that was not written in this book of the law, - not only those that were written in the book of the law, but those also that did not stand therein. The diseases of Egypt that were written in the book of the law include the murrain of cattle, the boils and blains, and the death of the first-born (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.1-Exod.9.10">Exo 9:1-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.12.29">Exo 12:29</reference>); and the strokes (מכּה) the rest of the plagues, viz., the frogs, gnats, dog-flies, hail, locusts, and darkness (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.10">Ex 8-10</reference>). יעלּם, an uncommon and harder form of יעלם (Jdg 16:3; cf. <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §138, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.).
entries.63ed95ebac3f593e2b01d22053dc626f0e4f87d1: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.62">Deu 28:62</reference> <div eID="gen2509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2510" type="x-p"/> Israel would be almost annihilated thereby. “<hi type="italic">Ye will be left in few people</hi> (a small number; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.26.5">Deu 26:5</reference>), <hi type="italic">whereas ye were as numerous as the stars of heaven</hi>.”
entries.9c73dd88cc17723f103ee926b56101de19977fdf: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.63">Deu 28:63</reference> <div eID="gen2510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2511" type="x-p"/> Yea, the Lord would find His pleasure in the destruction and annihilation of Israel, as He had previously rejoiced in blessing and multiplying it. With this bold anthropomorphic expression Moses seeks to remove from the nation the last prop of false confidence in the mercy of God. Greatly as the sin of man troubles God, and little as the pleasure may be which He has in the death of the wicked, yet the holiness of His love demands the punishment and destruction of those who despise the riches of His goodness and long-suffering; so that He displays His glory in the judgment and destruction of the wicked no less than in blessing and prospering the righteous.
entries.04d23b1d195c6dbb26c54eadac74a2d3e4d6f5d5: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.63-Deut.28.64">Deu 28:63-64</reference> <div eID="gen2511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2512" type="x-p"/> Those who had not succumbed to the plagues and strokes of God, would be torn from the land of their inheritance, and scattered among all nations to the end of the earth, and there be compelled to serve other gods, which are wood and stone, which have no life and no sensation, and therefore can hear no prayer, and cannot deliver out of any distress (cf. Deu 4:27.).
entries.21b4d9c38e81b6f163fdef07a79b94d83389b223: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.65-Deut.28.66">Deu 28:65-66</reference> <div eID="gen2512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2513" type="x-p"/> When banished thus among all nations, Israel would find no ease or rest, not even rest for the sole of its foot, i.e., no place where it could quietly set its foot, and remain and have peace in its heart. To this extreme distress of homeless banishment there would be added “<hi type="italic">a trembling heart, failing of the eyes</hi> (the light of life), <hi type="italic">and despair of soul</hi>” (vid., Lev 26:36.).
entries.b7cd0ae57658ab58473314ad78e8800efb72f7d8: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.66">Deu 28:66</reference> <div eID="gen2513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2514" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Thy life will be hung up before thee</hi>,” i.e., will be like some valued object, hanging by a thin thread before thine eyes, which any moment might tear down (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>), that is to say, will be ever hanging in the greatest danger. “<hi type="italic">Thou wilt not believe in thy life</hi>,” i.e., thou wilt despair of its preservation (cf. Job. <reference osisRef="Deut.24.22">Deu 24:22</reference>).<note placement="foot">“I have never seen a passage which describes more clearly the misery of a guilty conscience, in words and thoughts so fitting and appropriate. For this is just the way in which a man is affected, who knows that God is offended, i.e., who is harassed with the consciousness of sin”' (<hi type="italic">Luther</hi>).</note>
entries.526e503a6634130a382edca395d4e0487b8d70bc: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.67">Deu 28:67</reference> <div eID="gen2514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2515" type="x-p"/> In the morning they would wish it were evening, and in the evening would wish it were morning, from perpetual dread of what each day or night would bring.
entries.d7a7c6f9ea3e2cc85b4c80fb11e3df3275936b69: <reference osisRef="Deut.28.68">Deu 28:68</reference> <div eID="gen2515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2516" type="x-p"/> Last of all, Moses mentions the worst, namely, their being taken back to Egypt into ignominious slavery. “If the Exodus was the birth of the nation of God as such, return would be its death” (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>). “<hi type="italic">In ships:</hi>” i.e., in a way which would cut off every possibility of escape. The clause, “<hi type="italic">by the way whereof I spake unto thee, thou shalt see it no more again,</hi>” is not a more precise explanation of the expression “in ships,” for it was not in ships that Israel came out of Egypt, but by land, through the desert; on the contrary, it simply serves to strengthen the announcement, “The Lord shall bring thee into Egypt again,” namely, in the sense that God would cause them to take a road which they would never have been again if they had continued in faithful dependence upon the Lord. This was the way to Egypt, in reality such a return to this land as Israel ought never to have experienced, namely, a return to slavery. “<hi type="italic">There shall ye be sold to your enemies as servants and maids, and there shall be no buyer</hi>,” i.e., no one will buy you as slaves. This clause, which indicates the utmost contempt, is quite sufficient to overthrow the opinion of <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, <hi type="italic">Riehm</hi>, and others, already referred to at pp. 928, 929, namely, that this verse refers to Psammetichus, who procured some Israelitish infantry from Manasseh. Egypt is simply mentioned as a land where Israel had lived in ignominious bondage. “As a fulfilment of a certain kind, we might no doubt adduce the fact that Titus sent 17,000 adult Jews to Egypt to perform hard labour there, and had those who were under 17 years of age publicly sold (Josephus,<hi type="italic">de bell. Jud.</hi> vi. 9, 2), and also that under Hadrian Jews without number were sold at Rachel’s grave (<hi type="italic">Jerome, ad</hi> Jer 31). But the word of God is not so contracted, that it can be limited to one single fact. The curses were fulfilled in the time of the Romans in Egypt (vid., Philo in Flacc., and <hi type="italic">leg. ad Caium</hi>), but they were also fulfilled in a horrible manner during the middle ages (vid., <hi type="italic">Depping, die Juden im Mittelalter</hi>); and they are still in course of fulfilment, even though they are frequently less sensibly felt” (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>). Deu 28:69 <div eID="gen2516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2517" type="x-p"/> Is not the close of the address in ch. 5-28, as <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>, <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, and others suppose; but the heading to ch. 29-30, which relate to the making of the covenant mentioned in this verse (vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.29.12">Deu 29:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.14">Deu 29:14</reference>).  <chapter eID="Deut.28"/> <div eID="gen2517" type="x-p"/>

entries.b6dec236c8fb660ae5550a6f3c026f4183eb44ac: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.28.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.28.1" sID="gen16385" type="section"/><p/> <div sID="gen16386" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1. </hi><hi type="italic">And it shall come to pass, if thou shalt hearken</hi>. He teaches the same thing as before in different words; but the diversity of expression, as well as the repetition, tends to its confirmation. First, God says that He would deal with them so bountifully that they should excel all other nations; for this is the meaning of the words, that they should be illustrious above all the rest of the world on account of the special blessings of God. He afterwards enumerates the blessings which shall never depart from them, if they persevere in the service of God; and here it must be observed that they are reminded, not only in how many ways God is bountiful towards His servants, but also to how many necessities they are exposed, which require His direct and constant aid; for if we are blessed in the city and in the field, we can no more move a foot than stand still, except by His blessing. Such also is the tendency of the whole list, that a scarcity of all things impends over us at every moment, unless God should continually succor us by remedies sent down from heaven, and that every good thing can only come from that one source.<div eID="gen16386" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.28.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen16385" osisID="Deut.28.1" type="section"/>
entries.7b699c640aabc961411d7221bd96ae1d1f99e5d6: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.28.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.28.9" sID="gen16387" type="section"/> <div sID="gen16388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9. </hi><hi type="italic">The Lord shall establish thee a holy people unto himself</hi>. This refers indeed to earthly blessings, as if Moses said, that by them would be manifested God’s love towards His chosen people; still it rises higher, so that the Israelites, led on by degrees, should learn to embrace God alone, and to trust in Him according to the covenant which He had made with Abraham, “I am thy exceeding great reward.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.1">Genesis 15:1</reference>.) For the children of Abraham were set apart and chosen to be a holy people, not only in order that, being well fed, and with a full belly, they should aspire to nothing but earthly things, but that they might be confidently assured that they would be blessed in death as well as life. Although their adoption was gratuitous, still, inasmuch as they were called unto purity, it is not without reason that God promises that what He had spoken should be sure, if by keeping the Law the Israelites themselves should continue in the covenant; as much as to say, that their sanctification <note n="215"> <div sID="gen16389" type="x-p"/> “Leur election.” — <hi type="italic">Fr</hi>.<div eID="gen16389" type="x-p"/> </note> should be firm and perpetual if they walked in the commandments of the Law. When He adds that it should be manifest “to <note n="216"> <div sID="gen16390" type="x-p"/> “And all the people of the earth shall see that those are called by the name of the Lord.” — <hi type="italic">A</hi>.<hi type="italic">V</hi>. “And all peoples of the earth shall see that the name of Jehovah is called upon thee,” <hi type="italic">i</hi>.<hi type="italic">e</hi>., “thou art called by his name.” — Ainsworth.<div eID="gen16390" type="x-p"/> </note> all people of the earth that the name of God was called upon them,” it is equivalent to saying, that it should be known that they were under God’s defense and patronage, and that thus they should always be safe and secure in His protection.<div eID="gen16388" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.28.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen16387" osisID="Deut.28.9" type="section"/>
entries.b4c90fd224d5556218188196c87c3708b0f0853c:
12. The Lord shall open to thee his good treasure. He again repeats, that the goodness of God shines forth in many ways in the life of men, since He not only supplies the bread that they eat, but that the rain which descends from heaven waters the earth; and that thus He produces whatever is required for food from His plenteous store-house or treasure. Let us learn, therefore, both above and beneath, as well in the temperature of the atmosphere, in the quickening heat of the sun, in the rain, and in other means, as in the fertility of the earth, to contemplate the manifold riches which God brings forth from His treasures. And when He declares that He will bless the work of our hands, hence, too, let us learn that we can attain nothing by our industry and hardest labors, except in so far as God vouchsafes us good success; and that all our efforts without His secret blessing are mere useless fatigue. For the figure which Paul uses in reference to the spiritual culture of the Church, is taken from nature itself:
“Neither is he that planteth anything, neither he that watereth, but God that giveth the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:7.)
God would not, indeed, have
“Que nous demeurions assis, et lesjambes croissees comme des faineans;” that we should remain seated, with our legs crossed, like do-nothings. — Fr.
us lie idle, and therefore He requires the labor of our hands, but He would have the fruit of our labors attributed to Himself.
After having spoken of the whole Law, and forbidden that they should turn aside to the right or the left, He adverts to the principal point, i.e., that they should not revolt to strange gods. Wherefore, the sum comes to this, that, in order that God may continue to shew us the favor which He has begun towards us, we ought on our sides to be altogether submissive to His rule. This indeed He demands of us by His word, and enables us to perform it by the power of His Spirit; not, it is true, fully to do our duty, but to strive to reach the goal; and, whereas we are far from attaining perfection, His indulgence supplies what is wanting in us.
Here, however, a difficult question arises, — If all prosperity proceeds from the peculiar blessing which God vouchsafes to His servants, whence is it that many of His despisers have children, easy and happy circumstances, abundance of the fruits of fire earth, enjoyment and luxury, honors and power? I answer, that the happy condition of life, which He assigns to His servants, does not prevent Him from diffusing His bounty promiscuously over the whole human race. He is truly called in Psalm 36:6, the preserver of “man and beast.” It is said elsewhere,
See margin A.V., “Merciful, or bountiful in all his works.”
that His mercy is extended over all His creatures, (Psalm 145:17;) and justly does Christ exalt His unbounded goodness, in that “He maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.” (Matthew 5:45.) But equally true is the exclamation of the Prophet;
“Oh, how great is thy goodness, which thou hast laid up for them that fear thee!” (Psalm 31:19.)
For since all without exception enjoy all the supports of life, God’s goodness, which thus contends with the wickedness of men, shines forth universally even towards the ungodly, so that He does not cease to cherish and preserve those whom He has created, although they be unworthy. He therefore does good to the ungodly, because He is their Creator; besides, in order to keep the minds of believers in suspense in expectation of the final judgment, He now suffers many things to be confusedly mixed together, and hides His judgment in the darkness of night, as it were, or at least under clouds; whilst He also so tempers His patience towards the reprobate, as that, in this confusion of which I have spoken, some signs of His anger and favor are manifested. Thus, although the government of the world is not yet reduced to a perfect rule, still God shews by it that He is both the avenger of sins and the rewarder of righteousness, and some sparks are seen through the darkness; whilst the faithful, although they do not attain to the full enjoyment of the blessing promised them, nevertheless taste of it as far as is expedient. But to the ungodly, although they abound with all sorts of good things, not a single drop of God’s goodness is dispensed; for unless a sense of God’s paternal favor is awakened by His blessing, the blessing itself ceases to exist; nay, the more they gorge themselves, they attain to a deadly fatness; and God purposely lifts them up, that He may cast them down more heavily from their high estate. In a word, they are fed, as the Prophet says,
No reference is here given in the original. The allusion might be to Jeremiah 12:3, or 51:40.
“unto the day of slaughter.”
It must be concluded, therefore, that the blessings which God here promises to His servants are seasoned by Him with spiritual salt, lest they should be tasteless; whilst the reprobate, who are destitute of a sense of His grace, are also deprived altogether of all His blessings. There still, however, remains a difficulty, because the felicity here spoken of does not always, nor equally fall to the lot of God’s servants; nay, even under the Law they were sharply tried by many troubles and adversities. I answer, that since none, not even the most holy, was ever a perfect keeper of the Law, since none was ever free from all transgression, it is no cause of surprise that they only partially enjoyed the promised blessings; inasmuch as they were not fit recipients (capaces) of their fullness; and, if it sometimes happens that they are chastised more severely than the ungodly, neither in this is there any absurdity, since God usually begins His judgment at His own house. (Isaiah 10:12; 1 Peter 4:17.) Still, even in this confusion we see what the Prophet teaches, that the righteous are never forsaken, (Psalm 37:25,) and that they are like green and fruitful olive-trees in the courts of the Lord, (Psalm 52:8,) whilst the ungodly, although for a season they may be exalted like cedars of Lebanon, yet are plucked up in a moment by the roots, so that no trace of them remains.
Deuteronomy 7
Deuteronomy 7:9-15
